---
description: "A visual story about the Pacific share of world carbon dioxide emissions and the changes unfolding across its ocean and islands"
---

```{=html}
<header class="hero">
  <div class="hero-water" aria-hidden="true"></div>
  <div class="hero-inner">
    <p class="eyebrow">A Pacific climate data story</p>
    <h1>Living with a Changing Climate Across the Pacific</h1>
    <p class="hero-lede">The places in this story produced 0.0454% of world territorial CO₂ in 2023. Their ocean is warming, coral heat is spreading and a single cyclone can shake an entire national economy.</p>
    <div class="hero-pair" aria-label="Pacific and world territorial carbon dioxide emissions in 2023 from Our World in Data">
      <article>
        <span class="hero-place">17 Pacific places</span>
        <strong>17.3 million t</strong>
        <span>territorial CO₂ in 2023</span>
      </article>
      <article>
        <span class="hero-place">World</span>
        <strong>38.1 billion t</strong>
        <span>territorial CO₂ in 2023</span>
      </article>
    </div>
    <p class="hero-share"><strong>0.0454%</strong><span>of the world total came from the 17 Pacific island countries and territories in this comparison.</span></p>
  </div>
</header>

<nav class="chapter-nav" aria-label="Story chapters">
  <a href="#emissions">A tiny share</a>
  <a href="#impact">When storms hit</a>
  <a href="#cyclones">A crowded ocean</a>
  <a href="#warming">Warmer water</a>
  <a href="#reefs">Reefs under heat</a>
  <a href="#sea">A higher sea</a>
  <a href="#rain">Rain and harvests</a>
  <a href="#response">The energy shift</a>
</nav>

<main>
  <section id="emissions" class="chapter chapter-light">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">01</p>
      <h2>The Pacific share almost disappears</h2>
      <p>The 17 Pacific places shown here produced 17.3 million tonnes of territorial CO₂ in 2023. The world produced 38.1 billion tonnes. Put them on the same scale and the Pacific share is a sliver: 0.0454%, or roughly one tonne in every 2,200.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="emissions-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="Pacific and world territorial carbon dioxide emissions in 2023 at full scale and enlarged"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="impact" class="chapter chapter-impact">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">02</p>
      <h2>One cyclone can shake an entire economy</h2>
      <p>The scale changes when a cyclone reaches land. Across these four storms, assessments placed the economic blow between more than one fifth and nearly two thirds of annual GDP. Pam displaced 65,000 people in Vanuatu. Winston affected 540,400 people in Fiji.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="event-cards" class="event-grid" aria-label="Human and economic consequences of four Pacific cyclones"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="cyclones" class="chapter chapter-map">
    <div class="chapter-copy chapter-copy-map">
      <p class="chapter-number">03</p>
      <h2>Four storms sit inside a much larger web</h2>
      <p>From 1980 to 2023, 508 recorded storm tracks crossed the South Pacific. Of those, 103 reached Category 3 or above, about one in five. Scroll through the map to see Pam, Winston, Gita and Harold emerge from that wider record.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="cyclone-scrolly" class="scrolly">
      <div class="scrolly-sticky">
        <svg id="cyclone-map" viewBox="0 0 1000 600" role="img" aria-label="South Pacific tropical cyclone tracks from 1980 through 2023"></svg>
        <div id="cyclone-legend" class="map-legend"></div>
      </div>
      <div class="scrolly-steps">
        <article class="step" data-view="all">
          <p class="step-label">The wider record</p>
          <h3>Storm after storm has crossed the South Pacific</h3>
          <p>These 508 tracks show how widely cyclones have travelled across the region since 1980.</p>
        </article>
        <article class="step" data-view="intensity">
          <p class="step-label">The strongest tracks</p>
          <h3>About one in five reached Category 3 or above</h3>
          <p>The strongest 103 tracks weave through the same islands and waters.</p>
        </article>
        <article class="step" data-view="events">
          <p class="step-label">Four familiar names</p>
          <h3>Pam, Winston, Gita and Harold emerge from the web</h3>
          <p>Each highlighted line leads back to the lives and national economies shown in the cards above.</p>
        </article>
      </div>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section id="warming" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">04</p>
      <h2>The slower change reaches every place</h2>
      <p>Cyclones mark individual days. Ocean warming unfolds across decades. The sea surface average for 2014 to 2023 was warmer than the 1993 to 2002 average in every one of the 21 places. French Polynesia records the smallest shift at 0.21°C. Nauru records the largest at 0.49°C. Every row moves in the same direction.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="sst-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Early and recent sea surface temperature averages for 21 Pacific places"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="reefs" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">05</p>
      <h2>The heat reaches the reefs</h2>
      <p>Coral heat stress builds as unusually warm water lingers. In 2024, all eight stations crossed 4°C weeks, when significant bleaching can occur. Seven also crossed 8°C weeks, when severe bleaching and coral mortality become likely.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="reef-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Annual maximum Degree Heating Weeks at eight Pacific reef stations from 1985 to 2025"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="sea" class="chapter chapter-dark">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">06</p>
      <h2>By 2023, every row ends in a higher sea level band</h2>
      <p>The early years are filled with neutral bands and a few lower readings. Warmer colours spread across the chart over time. In 2023, all 21 records show a positive anomaly. Twenty sit at +0.1 metre and Vanuatu at +0.2 metre.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="sea-chart" class="viz-frame viz-frame-dark" role="img" aria-label="Sea level anomaly bands for 21 Pacific places from 1993 to 2023"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="rain" class="chapter chapter-light">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">07</p>
      <h2>Do wetter years bring better harvests?</h2>
      <p>The 450 observations give a messy answer. Wetter years include 124 yield gains and 105 losses. Drier years include 121 gains and 100 losses. The overall correlation is 0.04, so the points settle into a cloud instead of a clear slope.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="rain-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="Annual rainfall and crop yield changes across 450 observations in 15 Pacific places"></div>
  </section>

  <section id="response" class="chapter chapter-light chapter-response">
    <div class="chapter-copy">
      <p class="chapter-number">08</p>
      <h2>The move to renewable electricity is uneven</h2>
      <p>Tokelau sits at one end of the chart, with renewables supplying 94.4% of its electricity in 2023. Fiji is the only other place above halfway, at 52.1%. The next highest share is Papua New Guinea at 33.5%, and four places remain below 10%.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="energy-chart" class="viz-frame" role="img" aria-label="Renewable share of electricity generation in 18 Pacific places in 2023"></div>
  </section>

  <section class="closing">
    <p class="eyebrow">The full picture</p>
    <h2>So where does that leave the Pacific?</h2>
    <p>The story began with a sliver of world emissions. It moved through storms, warmer seas, stressed reefs, changing sea levels and unpredictable harvests. The final chart shows action already under way, with plenty of distance left to travel.</p>
  </section>

  <footer class="sources">
    <div class="source-inner">
      <p class="eyebrow">Sources</p>
      <h2>Where the numbers came from</h2>

        <p><a href="https://stats.pacificdata.org/vis?av=true&amp;df%5Bag%5D=SPC&amp;df%5Bds%5D=SPC2&amp;df%5Bid%5D=DF_CLIMATE_CHANGE&amp;df%5Bvs%5D=1.0&amp;lc=en">Pacific climate indicators</a><span>Sea surface temperature, sea level, annual rainfall and crop yield records</span></p>
        <p><a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/international-best-track-archive">NOAA IBTrACS version 4.01</a><span>South Pacific cyclone positions and recorded intensity from 1980 to 2023</span></p>
        <p><a href="https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/methodology.php">NOAA Coral Reef Watch</a><span>Annual maximum Degree Heating Weeks at eight virtual stations from 1985 to 2025</span></p>
        <p><a href="https://stats.pacificdata.org/vis?av=true&amp;df%5Bag%5D=SPC&amp;df%5Bds%5D=SPC2&amp;df%5Bid%5D=DF_POWER_GEN&amp;df%5Bvs%5D=1.0&amp;dq=A...&amp;lc=en">Pacific power generation</a><span>Renewable electricity and generation from other sources in 2023</span></p>
        <p class="source-bundle"><strong>Cyclone event assessments</strong><a href="https://www.dfat.gov.au/sites/default/files/post-disaster-needs-assessment-cyclone-pam.pdf">Pam</a><a href="https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/143591490296944528/pdf/113710-NWP-PUBLIC-P159592-1701.pdf">Winston</a><a href="https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/356451584939594362/pdf/Post-Disaster-Rapid-Assessment-Tropical-Cyclone-Gita.pdf">Gita</a><a href="https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/289451643709153886/pdf/Dealing-with-Disasters-Analyzing-Vanuatu-s-Economy-and-Public-Finances-Through-the-Lens-of-Disaster-Resilience.pdf">Harold</a><span>People, displacement, economic effects and GDP figures for each event</span></p>
      </div>
      <section class="source-notes" aria-labelledby="number-notes-title">
        <h3 id="number-notes-title">Notes on the numbers</h3>
        <div class="source-notes-grid">
          <p class="source-method">The emissions comparison uses territorial CO₂ for 2023 from one Our World in Data release. It covers the 17 Pacific places with a value for that year. Five places in the project list had no 2023 value. Consumption emissions, land use change and other greenhouse gases sit outside this measure.</p>
          <p class="source-method">Each cyclone assessment uses its own terms, so affected people, displaced people, damage and wider economic effects remain separate. The track map uses the USA Saffir Simpson category in IBTrACS and begins in 1980, within the modern satellite era. A study of cyclone trends would need its own analysis.</p>
          <p class="source-method">Degree Heating Weeks is a satellite measure of accumulated heat stress. Observations at the reef provide evidence of bleaching. Sea level values arrive rounded to 0.1 metre, while local shorelines also respond to waves, storms, sediment and land movement.</p>
          <p class="source-method">The electricity chart covers generation. Transport and other energy uses are recorded separately. The reproducible tidyverse data build is in <a href="r/build_story.R">r/build_story.R</a>. Derived tables are stored in the story folder. Sources were accessed on 9 August 2026.</p>
        </div>
      </section>
      <p class="site-credit">Built with love and curiosity using R and Quarto by <a href="https://edodanilyan.com">Edo Danilyan</a>.</p>
    </div>
  </footer>
</main>
```
